name: Stack-TS-TW

frames.best_why: The top photo sits flat and fully visible with the fanned deck clearly poking out behind it.

tagline: A deck of square photos fans out, and the top card swipes away.
summary: A small deck of square photo cards stacked with a slight fan. Drag the top card off to throw it to the back of the pile, or click it to shuffle it under while a spring settles the rest.
appearance: A stack of square photos with rounded corners: the front card flat and full-size while the ones behind poke out at the top-right, each nudged a few degrees and slightly smaller. On a near-black stage a line of grey helper text sits below the pile.
behaviour: Dragging the front card tilts it in 3D and, past a set distance, throws it to the back of the deck; a spring fans the remaining cards into place. Clicking also sends the card back, and an optional autoplay cycles them on a timer.
demo_content: Square nature photos: a wave, a glass terrarium of plants, and an ageing car beside a stone building.
search_phrases: drag cards to the back of the pile
stacked photos you can throw away
3d photo deck on a dark stage
click a card to shuffle it behind
fanned deck of pictures with spring
use_when: You want a tactile little gallery or testimonial deck a visitor can flip through by dragging the top card away.
avoid_when: It needs a sized square-ish container, and the drag or click has no keyboard equivalent.
customise: You pass an array of cards (any nodes, usually images) plus sensitivity, autoplay timing, click-to-send-back, random rotation, spring stiffness and a mobile breakpoint. Card styling is your own.
weight_why: A handful of motion-driven cards that only animate when swiped or on the optional autoplay timer.

a11y.note: Cards are plain divs with no keyboard focus or arrow-key support, and the spring swipe ignores reduced-motion.

issues: The cards are not focusable or operable from the keyboard, so the deck is pointer-only.
The stack is h-full, so it collapses to nothing if its wrapper has no set height.
polish_why: Clean photo deck with a satisfying spring swipe, but plain image cards and a thin demo.
